main.chip.archive.tip:
• The archive chip has no size ceiling.
• The engine spends bits up to visually lossless quality and stops there.
• While this chip is on, the number in the target box does not build the plan.
• The file does get smaller, but the source decides how much, not you.
• If you have to fit somewhere, pick one of the chips that names an MB figure.
• Touching the target brings the size ceiling back.

main.chip.whatsapp.label: WhatsApp recommended
main.chip.whatsapp.tip:
• WhatsApp re-encodes in-chat video with its own low-bitrate encoder.
• Under 16 MB it usually passes your file through with far less damage, so what the other side sees is VidShrink's quality, not WhatsApp's.
• To bypass re-encoding entirely, send the result as a document instead of as a video.

main.chip.25.tip: 25 MB fits Gmail attachments and most ticket systems.
main.chip.100.tip: 100 MB suits archiving and uploads where quality matters more than transfer time.
main.chip.134.label: Sharing maximum
main.chip.134.tip:
• 134 MB is the measured ceiling of uguu.se, the anonymous share target with the smallest limit.
• A file at or under this size can be handed to either share target without being refused.
• The other target, storage.to, carries far more, so this chip is the safe number for both.
main.chip.180.label: WhatsApp Web maximum
main.chip.180.tip:
• On the phone: 16 MB in chat, 2 GB as a document.
• WhatsApp Web takes 180 MB per file. The user reports this, WhatsApp does not publish it.
• So a file of 180 MB or less goes through the web side as it is.

main.output.title: Output
main.output.estimated-time.tip:
• VidShrink times the sample encodes it already ran on this clip, so the speed behind this figure comes from this machine and this file, not from a preset table.
• Two-pass runs get a wide range because the first pass only analyses the picture and costs less than the second, and how much less is not measured.
• If the plan moves to settings the samples were not encoded with, the time is left blank, not guessed.
main.output.estimated-output.tip:
• Before planning, VidShrink encodes short samples of this clip at two resolutions.
• It measures how many bits the clip really needs.
• Until then, or if the sample fails, the estimate uses the source bitrate.
• The note under the estimate says which of the two it is.
• Two-pass runs land within a few percent.
• Hardware encoders run a single pass and can come in under the target.
• Quality-capped runs come in under the target on purpose, because spending the rest would buy nothing you could see.

main.convert.title: Conversion
main.convert.source-empty: Load a source in Shrink or browse here.
main.convert.container.tip:
• The container is the file type.
• MP4 is the safest general choice and the only one WhatsApp reliably sends as a playable video — every phone opens it.
• MKV supports many stream types but WhatsApp and most phone galleries treat it as a document.
• WebM is for browsers and is not a phone format.
• MOV suits Apple workflows and plays on iPhone, but Android support is uneven.
• AVI is for older software only.
• MP3, M4A, and WAV create audio-only files.
main.convert.video-codec.tip:
• H.264 plays on nearly every device and is what WhatsApp expects; pick it when the file must just work.
• H.265 makes files a third smaller at the same picture; phones since 2016 decode it in hardware.
• But older handsets, some smart TVs, and several web players will not open it, and WhatsApp may re-encode it.
• VP9 is a browser and WebM format; phones play it in apps but rarely in the gallery.
• AV1 compresses best and is the slowest to encode, and only recent phones decode it.
• Copy keeps the original video untouched — no quality loss, no waiting — if the container accepts it.
main.convert.quality-mode.tip:
• CRF targets visual quality, so final size can vary.
• Fixed bitrate targets a data rate, so size is predictable.
• Use CRF for normal viewing quality and fixed bitrate when size or bandwidth matters more.
main.convert.crf-label.tip:
• In CRF mode, a lower number means higher quality and a larger file; 23 is a common H.264 start.
• In fixed bitrate mode, enter kilobits per second: a higher value gives more quality and a larger file.
main.convert.resolution.tip:
• Source keeps the original dimensions.
• A numbered option limits output height while preserving aspect ratio.
• Lower resolution reduces file size and processing load.
• Custom allows an exact width and height.
main.convert.custom-resolution.tip:
• Used only when resolution is custom.
• Enter width and height as 1280x720.
• Even dimensions are safest for common video codecs.
main.convert.frame-rate.tip:
• Source preserves the original frame rate.
• 60 is smoother but needs more data.
• 30 suits most video.
• 24 gives a cinema-like motion style.
• Reducing frame rate can reduce file size.
main.convert.custom-fps.tip:
• Used only when frame rate is custom.
• Enter the frames per second, such as 25 or 29.97.
• Values above the source frame rate usually add no real motion detail.
main.convert.audio.tip:
• AAC is the safe pairing for MP4 and the only codec every phone and WhatsApp accept.
• Opus sounds better at low bitrates but belongs in WebM; inside MP4 it will not play on many phones.
• MP3 suits older players.
• PCM is uncompressed and very large.
• Copy preserves the original audio without re-encoding when the container supports it.
• Drop removes audio completely, which is the right call when you are squeezing a silent clip.
main.convert.audio-bitrate.tip:
• Audio data rate in kilobits per second.
• 128 is a compact general setting, 192 provides more detail, and 256 or 320 is useful for music.
• This value is ignored for copy, drop, and raw PCM.
main.convert.trim-start.tip:
• Optional trim start time.
• Leave empty to begin at the start of the source.
• Use hours:minutes:seconds, for example 00:01:30.
main.convert.trim-end.tip:
• Optional trim end time.
• Leave empty to continue to the end of the source.
• The end time must be later than the start time.

main.about.title: About VidShrink
main.about.intro:
• VidShrink is an offline tool for target-size video compression and format conversion.
• Give it a file and a size ceiling; it works out the settings that lose the least of what a person can actually see, and never returns a file larger than you asked for.
main.about.engine.title: How the Engine Thinks
main.about.engine.body:
• Most size-target compressors apply a fixed table: this many megabytes per minute becomes that resolution.
• That table is wrong for every clip that is not average.
• VidShrink measures instead. It encodes short samples of your actual file at two resolutions and reads how many bits it really costs, and how much of that cost disappears when the picture is scaled down.
• Those two measurements make the plan specific to this clip rather than to video in general.
main.about.measured.title: Measured, not assumed
main.about.measured.table:
complexity      measured from your file, not its bitrate
detail falloff  measured; decides if scaling down is worth it
resolution      continuous search, not a fixed ladder
frame rate      searched alongside resolution, not after it
codec           chosen from how hard the target actually is
audio           share of budget shrinks as the target tightens
estimate        a measured number with a range, shown up front
main.about.loss.title: Where the Loss Goes
main.about.loss.body:
• Below a certain bit budget something has to give.
• The engine spends the loss where the eye is least sensitive: softness before blocking, fewer pixels before broken pixels, mono audio before a starved picture.
• It also knows when to stop — once quality reaches the point where more bits buy nothing you could see, it hands back a smaller file instead of padding it to the target.
main.about.scenario.title: Scenario awareness
main.about.scenario.body:
• A 1.2x reduction and a 600x reduction are not the same problem, so they do not get the same treatment.
• Light targets keep everything and simply spend the budget.
• Balanced targets allow scaling.
• Aggressive and extreme targets unlock frame-rate reduction, move to H.265, and cut the audio share — and the app tells you what it changed and why, in plain language, before you press start.
main.about.ai.title: AI mode
main.about.ai.body:
• AI mode only creates a prompt and validates pasted JSON.
• No AI is embedded, so VidShrink works offline, asks for no API key, and falls back to the complete automatic engine when an answer is malformed or incompatible.
main.about.codecs.title: Codecs
main.about.codecs.body:
• H.264 offers the broadest compatibility.
• H.265 compresses more efficiently.
• VP9 is a strong WebM choice.
• AV1 maximizes modern compression at higher CPU cost.
• Stream copy is fastest and lossless when the destination supports the source streams.

main.advice.extreme-ratio: Extreme compression: loss is unavoidable, so the engine pushes it where it is least noticeable.
main.advice.below-codec-floor: This target is genuinely too small for this source: no layout reaches the bits per pixel the encoder needs for a meaningful picture. The densest layout was taken, but the result will look visibly broken; raising the target is the only real fix.
main.advice.frame-rate-for-floor: At the source frame rate every frame would fall below the density the encoder needs, so the frame rate was cut and the freed bits went to the frames that remain.
main.advice.motion-cut-cheap: The measurement shows little motion in this clip, so cutting the frame rate frees a lot of bits and the loss is hard to notice.
main.advice.motion-cut-expensive: The measurement shows heavy motion in this clip, so dropping frames buys little and resolution is cut before the frame rate is.
main.advice.content-simple: The content measured as simple, so the target is met with room to spare.
main.advice.content-complex: The content measured as detail-heavy, which is why the bit budget is tight.
main.advice.scale-saves-much: Scaling down frees a lot of bits on this particular clip.
main.advice.scale-saves-little: Scaling down frees little on this clip, so resolution is preserved.
main.advice.resolution-reduced: Resolution was lowered so the picture fits the budget.
main.advice.frame-rate-reduced: Frame rate was lowered to free bits for the frames that remain.
main.advice.two-pass: Two-pass encoding is used so the target size is actually hit.
main.advice.single-pass: This hardware encoder runs a single pass: bitrate control steers toward the target size, without a second pass.
main.advice.quality-ceiling: The quality ceiling was reached; the remaining budget is left unspent because it would buy nothing you could see.
main.advice.audio-reduced: The audio bitrate was lowered so more bits are left for the picture.
main.advice.audio-mono: Audio was folded to mono — inaudible on a phone speaker, and it buys bits for the picture.
main.advice.encoder-fallback-gpu: Fast shrink (GPU) is on but no working hardware encoder was found, so encoding fell back to a software encoder and there is no speed gain.
main.advice.encoder-fallback-hardware: A different hardware encoder is used instead of the preferred one; encoding still runs on hardware.
main.advice.encoder-fallback-not-in-buil: The preferred encoder is not part of this ffmpeg build; falling back to a software encoder.
main.advice.encoder-fallback-not-measure: The preferred encoder has not been measured on this machine; falling back to a software encoder.
main.advice.encoder-fallback-not-working: The preferred encoder could not be used on this machine; falling back to a software encoder.
main.advice.hdr-tonemapped: The source is HDR but the selected encoder cannot preserve 10-bit, so it was tone-mapped to SDR BT.709.
